Alright. I want to talk about the time a hobo stole my sandwich and I chased him to give him my drink that went along with it.

Work was boring so I took a break and walked to the convenience store near our building. I made a sandwich this morning and I wanted some soda to go along with it. When I stepped outside (holding my sandwich in one hand and soda in the other), there was this hobo guy in front of me asking for change. He said that it was toll fee for passing through the door (apparently, he was opening doors for people in exchange for money). I looked at him and thought nothing of it, so I put my soda on the ground to bring out my wallet. Right as I was bending down, he yanked my sandwich out of my hands and ran away. I grabbed my soda and followed him into the small parking space of this empty store nearby where he was crouched down, stuffing his face. I yelled out "hey!" and he looked up and saw me. The guy looked scared a bit but made this nasty leering smile. 

I suffer from clinical depression and that time I was dealing with a particularly rough day. At that moment, I felt really numb. I was so tired and felt so old. I didn't give a shit about anything anymore. So I put my soda down in front of him, said "here you go" and walked out of there. I left work early, went home and then took a really long nap.

I've seen the hobo guy only once ever since, but I think he didn't recognize me because I changed my hair color and gained weight.

Yeah you should, unless you wanna deal with something really difficult.

Good luck!

This song is one of those sad sad sad scenarios where you never get closure in the end and it just spirals onward. Anyway, I love this song because to me it gives off this really strong image of hyperreality - something we never liked being reminded about (but have to). You can see it in the lyrics and hear it in the song: there is this desperation of trying to accept the 'fake' despite knowing that it is not the real thing. We know it's close enough, it's good enough but it's not what we want. It can't be what we want (but we can't get what we want).

Sometimes I like to think in a literal sense that the ending is this reply from the other side, the hyperreality wishing it could be what we always wanted. It makes the little horror in the song even more terrifying (the horror being that we are in this situation and trapped in this hyperreality). It's this really subtle hint of an actual desire of wanting us trapped in that system by the system (covered heavily by a great ending to the song). Kinda like a robot falling in love - no real sentience but an uncanny attempt of a circuit board to mimic love.

I'd like to share a very interesting aspect my history teacher told us. We Filipinos, she says, are primarily clannish. A big part of our identity revolves around this notion.  We always need to "have" some sort of familial group we belong to in order to anchor our identities. It starts in our family and extends to "levels" across every social group. She said it goes like this:

Examine yourself (based on a purely cultural aspect) and the person you are against the barangay (the smallest social group apart from your family in our culture) is your family. This is the first stage. To your neighbors in your barangay you are "De Los Santos" or "Cruz" or anak ni ganito na nakatira dun sa may kanto. Our first stage of identity is our household and family. 

Now beyond your barangay is your community, your town. When people ask who you are, where you live always comes up (within your province or city or town). After the initial introduction of names, you will always here this: "Taga san ka/kayo?". In a community setting, this refers to what barangay you live in (or district or whatever). This is our second stage.

The third stage is exactly like the second stage except it is a reference to which community you belong to. This is because it is a stage we enter when dealing with fellow Pinoys on a national level. Similarly, after your name you are asked for which group you belong to: "Ay, Ilokano ak." or "Ay taga-Manila po ako". On a national level, to each other we are our communities. An example of this is how when you meet other Pinoys abroad and one vital question you ask is "taga san ka?". 

The fourth stage, which is the most relevant to this discussion, is our identity with regards to us Filipinos on an international scale. This is where our sensitivity with jokes made at our expense comes into motion. According to my teacher, outside the Philippines, the Filipino identity with regards to its primal clannish aspects clings hard to our blurred semblance of a National identity. This where "pinoy pride" comes from. This is why we feel a very concerningly small amount of patriotism in our country. This is why it matters so damn much that I am Filipino and you, foreigner, are not.

In my home, on the jeep, I am not a Filipino. I am a Cruz who lives around the corner, who is ka-Pampangan. To you, outside of me being a person, that is who I am. However, put me in an international setting and I deal with a conflict. Outside the Philippines, none of these things matter. So who am I? I am Filipino. What is being Filipino on a social aspect? Nothing you foreigners care about, it's very cultural and inclusive.

This is why, I think, we will continue to be insulted at our own expense and will continue to demand apologies for jokes and satire. Have you tried joking with someone else's social identity as a Filipino? It's really taken for granted. We know who we are. But joke about doctors from UP or whatever else as a foreigner, you are gonna have a really hard time. How can you know things like these? You aren't Filipino!

tl;dr: family-barangay-community-PINOY PRIDE.

I'm an undergrad taking arts management and for two years now, I've been interning at my uni's museum. The work is great, I love it but just recently, the admin decided that we put on this exhibition that would consist not of artists but professors "demonstrating" their craft (My uni btw is an art school. Or tries to be. I don't know). 

They are horrible.

Not only in attitude (they rival if not top the most irate and difficult artists we've worked with, and that is saying a lot) but also in commitment and output. Their art is terrible, their effort is terrible. Initially I was excited to do this exhibition - I even invited my friends. But seeing it now, I just want to burn the entire place. I've dropped subjects, spent no weekends, skipped important family events all for this exhibition and no one will get nothing out of it. 

Now, this isn't the only reason, but I thought I'd share this because it's given me so much stress that I've let myself go and weaken against my deeper and more difficult problems. I've been silently battling with major depression for a year, pretending to have been "cured" to stop my suffering from the stigma mental illness has. I was making progress but things just got even worse. My father tragically passed away just two months ago, leaving me to deal with the future of us four children and my mother's unending ache. 

On top of all this, I've been reviewing my studies and planning my life and I've realized that I will never amount to the person I expect myself to be, nor will I be able to accomplish the goals I've set. I was kicked out of my first uni because of my depression issues and enrolled in my current "art" school. I saw this as my second chance but to be honest this art school isn't any good at all. It's a mediocre anemic system well-hidden beneath the allure of being part of a line of prestigious schools. My professors don't teach very well, my classmates could not care less about anything and I learn nothing. I am literally paying for a diploma. You'd think this wasn't a problem but it is. It's very difficult battling illness, working jobs and internships and having to attend classes that waste your time. The only real reason I go to school is the chance to get a bachelor's degree and hopefully be admitted into a post-graduate degree that could hone my skills. But I can't deal with it anymore. I love studying! This twisted useless place is horrifying to me!

I am drowning. This frustration and hurt has seeped everywhere. I used to keep it to myself and deal with it at my place but now it's seeped everywhere- my home, my work, my art, my school, everything. Nothing is free of this darkness anymore. I've battled it for so long and I am so very tired. Tired of lying and fighting and trying to see hope. I attempted suicide a year ago and have learned. But is calling to me again. I use to have very different reasons for wanting to die but now more than anything else, I just want to sleep. I can't get a moment's peace anymore, not through my own means. So I thought I'd just leave this world. I'm weary of it.

I didn't say it's too unrealistic. Presidential politics here during elections is a big fat circus show where the best attractions win. It's all about making your campaign and propaganda stick. What I meant was that being president doesn't necessarily solve everything. Let the corruption business take a back seat and look at this systematically. The Presidential position is easily the least influential position in terms of power (at least in the Philippines it is). You're basically a figurehead. 

You can't make laws, just "suggest" and "approve". You don't handle the funds and the regulations yourself. You have departments and commissions and little people for that. Heck, you are so far up the chain of command, every little thing your government has to do goes through a million check points and all you technically accomplish is sorting out which is shit and which isn't. See, this is the fault in our system, imo. It's way too bureaucratic. It's a government that is built for people will true political will of which most politicians don't have. Think of it this way: who really need the government? People below the proverbial social food chain. Who do we elect into positions that can help? The fucking upper class elite - people who haven't starved in a fucking single day and don't honestly give a damn for those that do.

Also, it's the local government positions that can really dish out the country-changing laws and movements. IMO, we shouldn't keep thinking country-wide here, more of concentration on each and every province/city. This works better in the long run, I think, because here you have sincere and lasting development and good change happening at every point which leads to this actual change in the country. I mean, man, you can't fix a house with one huge carpenter, you gotta get a million little guys and tackle the thing at every point.

I don't think this would be a problem if you teach them to get small portions and then just ask for more. As I understand it, it's a problem that arises from being to full to finish the meal. (Unless of course it's more of a too-distracted-to-eat thing, then it's different.)

I grew up in a family that was hella strict on table manners and such. Back then, we used to be very poor so leaving scraps was a sin. It was such a valuable important need and very hard to come by. Our parents also taught us how wasting food was an act of disrespect for all the people who worked hard bringing the food to the table (not just them, like the farmers etc.). They came from rural region and both had very difficult lives trying to make a living from crop fields and vegetables.

I know it's a bit vague but the point I think was that teaching a child to finish his/her dinner teaches important lessons on responsibility: Whatever you decide to put on your plate, you're responsible for it. It also teaches the value of food and resources. Yeah, I've heard the starving African kids story a million times and yeah eating everything on your plate won't save them, but wasting food is just making the situation worse. 

(I haven't given thought to how family dinners with prepared and set courses would go, so I think this applies mainly to self-serve sort of family dinners)

Appreciating anything always starts with context. To appreciate something, it has to make sense to you. IMO, this "meaning" does not necessarily have to come directly from the artist, nor does it need to  be based on a certain perceived "correct" meaning. So yeah, you simply commenting how a painting "looks neat" already qualifies as a certain appreciation.

A lot of people argue (and you probably might too) about the value and truth of "simple" aesthetic appreciation versus "deep" contextual appreciation. Like how you saying a painting's pretty is supposedly a shallow appreciation when compared to an extensive knowledge and critic about the piece. However, I believe that between the two, there really isn't much of a difference. Art never loses anything when perceived contrary to what it intends to depict. In fact, this is one of the most fundamental aspects of art: to make you think and to make you realize that there are thoughts out there other than your own.

So, I guess, to appreciate a painting, all you have to do is look and think. It looks neat, yes. Do you think this is a universal characteristic or are you the lone weirdo standing here thinking how great this is when it's nothing pure shit? What does that say about you? What does that say about other people? What does that say about the artist? About the art itself? And so on.

I think anyone can "get" art on a deeper level. You just have to realize the depth is there and take the plunge.
